Noahic Covenant: A rainbow becomes the sign of a promise made after the flood. The covenant includes Noah, his descendants, and every living creature, extending beyond the family that survived in the ark.
Abrahamic Covenant: Land, descendants, and blessing form the promises given to Abraham across these passages. The covenant also introduces circumcision as a sign, while its promised blessing reaches beyond Abraham's own family.
Sinai / Mosaic Covenant: Israel accepts a shared commitment at Sinai after Moses reads the covenant's words. These passages connect God's call for obedience with the people's promise to follow the instructions they have heard.
Priestly Covenant with Phinehas: Following Phinehas's action among the Israelites, God announces a covenant of peace. The promise gives his family a lasting place in the priesthood, linking his descendants to the event described in Numbers.
Davidic Covenant: The promise to David concerns his royal line as well as his own reign. These passages describe an enduring kingdom and recall the covenant through the language of a later psalm.
New Covenant: A promise in Jeremiah describes God's law becoming part of people's inner lives. Luke and Hebrews revisit that promise, connecting it with Jesus and contrasting the new covenant with the earlier one.
Aaronic Blessing: Israel's priests receive words to speak over the people in blessing. The passage presents God's care, favor, and peace as the gifts Aaron and his sons are instructed to ask for.
The Creation: Light, land and living creatures take shape as God orders the world in six days. Humanity receives responsibility for other creatures. On the seventh day, God rests and sets the day apart.
The Fall of Man: After eating the forbidden fruit, the man and woman hide and face God's questions. God announces pain, hard labor and death. They leave Eden, where guards block access to the tree of life.
Cain and Abel: Two brothers bring offerings, but only Abel's is accepted. Cain ignores God's warning and kills him. Exile follows, along with a protective mark against revenge.
The Line of Seth: A family record connects Adam and Seth to Noah and his three sons. It lists births, ages and deaths. Enoch's account differs because God takes him, while Noah's name expresses hope for relief.
Noah and the Flood: An ark carries Noah's family and animals through waters that cover the land. After leaving it, Noah builds an altar. God promises that no flood will again destroy all flesh, with a rainbow as the sign.
The Family of Noah: After the flood, an incident in Noah's vineyard leads to words concerning his sons and Canaan. The family record then traces his descendants into separate peoples, with their own lands and languages.
The Tower of Babel: Builders in Shinar use a shared language to raise a city and a tower reaching toward heaven. God makes their speech impossible to understand. Work stops, and the people scatter across the earth.
The Call of Abram: Following a stay in Haran, Abram answers God's call to travel to Canaan with Sarai and Lot. God promises descendants and blessings for other families. Abram builds altars along the way.
Abram and Lot: Disputes over grazing land lead Abram and Lot to separate, with Lot choosing the plain near Sodom. When invading kings take Lot captive, Abram rescues him. He later refuses the king of Sodom's goods.
Hagar and Ishmael: Conflict with Sarai sends the pregnant Hagar into the wilderness. An angel finds her beside a spring and promises many descendants. Hagar returns to Abram's household, where she gives birth to Ishmael.
Abraham and Sarah’s Covenant: God gives Abram and Sarai new names and promises that Sarah will bear Isaac. Circumcision becomes the covenant's sign. Later, Sarah laughs when visitors announce a son despite her old age.
Lot Leaves Sodom: Lot and his daughters escape Sodom, while his wife becomes a pillar of salt. Later, the daughters make their father drunk and conceive children by him. Their sons are Moab and Ben-ammi.
Isaac and Ishmael: Isaac's birth brings laughter to Sarah, but conflict later sends Hagar and Ishmael away. Their water runs out in the wilderness. God hears the boy and shows Hagar a well, and Ishmael grows up there.
The Binding of Isaac: On a mountain, Abraham prepares to sacrifice his son Isaac as God has commanded. A messenger stops him before the killing. Abraham offers a ram instead, and the promise of many descendants is repeated.
Isaac and Rebekah: A woman at a well offers water to Abraham's servant and his camels, matching the sign he requested. She is Rebekah, from Abraham's family. She agrees to travel with him and marry Isaac.
Jacob and Esau: Esau trades his birthright for food, and Jacob later gains their father's blessing by pretending to be his brother. Rebekah helps with the deception. Esau's anger follows, and Jacob leaves to find a wife.
Jacob’s Household: Seven years of work for Rachel lead first to Jacob's marriage to Leah, then to Rachel. Rivalry shapes their growing family. Leah, Rachel and their servants bear children, with Joseph born to Rachel.
Jacob Returns to Canaan: After leaving Laban, Jacob prepares to face the brother he fears. A night of wrestling leaves him injured and renamed Israel. Esau embraces him at their reunion, and the brothers go separate ways.
Dinah at Shechem: Shechem's sexual assault on Dinah leads to marriage negotiations between their households. Her brothers deceive the city, then kill its men and take captives. Jacob fears the attack will bring retaliation against his family.
The Death of Rachel: At Bethel, Jacob builds an altar and receives renewed promises of land and descendants. Rachel dies while giving birth during the journey. Jacob names their son Benjamin, and later joins Esau in burying Isaac.
Joseph and His Brothers: A favored son's dreams deepen a family conflict, and Joseph's brothers sell him to traders. They use his bloodstained coat to mislead Jacob. While his father mourns, Joseph is sold again in Egypt.
Judah and Tamar: Judah fails to arrange Tamar's promised marriage after his sons die. Disguised, she receives his seal, cord and staff. These identify him as the father of her pregnancy, and she later bears twins.
Joseph in Egypt: From Potiphar's household to prison, Joseph gains attention for interpreting dreams. Pharaoh's dreams bring him a new role. He stores grain during years of plenty to prepare Egypt for the famine ahead.
Joseph Reunites His Family: Food shortages bring Joseph's brothers before him in Egypt, where they fail to recognize him. After testing them, he reveals himself. Jacob's household moves to Goshen, and Joseph provides food during the famine.
Jacob Blesses His Family: Before dying, Jacob blesses his family and asks to be buried in Canaan. Joseph later reassures his brothers and provides for them. At his own death, he requests that his bones eventually leave Egypt.
Israel Oppressed in Egypt: A new Egyptian king fears Israel's growing numbers and imposes forced labor. Two midwives refuse his order to kill newborn boys. Pharaoh then commands his people to throw Hebrew sons into the river.
The Birth and Rescue of Moses: A basket hidden among river reeds carries a Hebrew baby to Pharaoh's daughter. His sister arranges for their mother to nurse him. The princess later raises the child as her son and names him Moses.
Moses Flees to Midian: After killing an Egyptian, Moses escapes Pharaoh's threat and settles in Midian. He helps Reuel's daughters, marries Zipporah and has a son. Meanwhile, Israel cries out under slavery, and God hears them.
The Burning Bush: While tending a flock, Moses encounters fire that leaves a bush unharmed. God sends him to bring Israel out of Egypt. Moses questions his ability, and God provides signs and Aaron's help as spokesman.
Moses Returns to Egypt: With his family and staff, Moses sets out from Midian for Egypt. Zipporah circumcises their son during a dangerous encounter. Aaron joins Moses, and their message and signs lead Israel's elders to believe.
Moses and Aaron Before Pharaoh: A request to let Israel worship brings harsher demands from Pharaoh, who withholds straw but keeps the brick quota. Israel's officers blame Moses. God renews the promise of freedom as the people's suffering continues.
The Plagues of Egypt: Nine disasters strike Egypt as Moses and Aaron seek Israel's release, from blood in the Nile to darkness. Pharaoh offers limited terms, then withdraws them. The dispute continues over who and what may leave.
The Passover and the Death of the Firstb: Israel prepares a lamb and marks doorposts with blood before Egypt's firstborn die at midnight. Pharaoh then orders the people out. They leave with unleavened dough, livestock and goods received from the Egyptians.
The Exodus from Egypt: Guided by cloud and fire, Israel leaves slavery by a route that avoids the Philistines' land. Moses carries Joseph's bones. Rules for unleavened bread and firstborn children preserve the memory of their departure.
Crossing the Sea: With Pharaoh's army behind them, Israel reaches the sea and fears death. Divided waters open a path across dry ground, then close over the pursuers. Moses and Miriam lead songs celebrating the rescue.
Bitter Water, Manna and Quail: Bitter water becomes drinkable, but hunger brings fresh complaints during Israel's journey. Quail and manna provide food. Rules for gathering manna include a double portion before the Sabbath, with a measure kept as a reminder.
Water from the Rock and the Battle with: Thirst brings quarrels at Rephidim, where water flows after Moses strikes a rock. An attack by Amalek follows. Joshua leads the battle while Aaron and Hur support Moses's raised hands until victory.
Jethro Advises Moses: Seeing Moses hear disputes alone, Jethro warns that the work will exhaust both him and the people. Moses adopts his advice. Appointed leaders hear smaller cases, while difficult matters still come to Moses.
The Covenant and Ten Commandments at Sin: Fire, thunder and a trumpet mark God's appearance at Sinai as Israel prepares below. The people hear commands about worship and daily conduct. Afraid, they ask Moses to speak to them instead.
The Covenant Is Sealed at Sinai: Israel agrees to the covenant after hearing Moses read its words, and blood marks the agreement. Moses and the elders ascend Sinai. He then enters the cloud for forty days and nights.
The Golden Calf: Aaron fashions a calf from gold while Moses remains on the mountain, and the people celebrate before it. Moses destroys the image and breaks the tablets. Killings and a plague follow as he seeks forgiveness.
Moses Sees God's Glory: Moses asks for God's presence on the journey and a glimpse of divine glory. New tablets replace the broken ones. After covenant instructions are renewed, Moses returns with a shining face and uses a veil.
Building the Tabernacle: Willing gifts supply skilled workers with more materials than the sanctuary needs. Moses inspects the completed work before it is assembled. God's glory fills the tabernacle, and the cloud guides Israel's movements.
Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained: A seven-day ceremony prepares Aaron and his sons for service as priests through washing, clothing and anointing. Their first sacrifices follow on the eighth day. Fire from God consumes the altar offering.
Nadab and Abihu: Unauthorized fire brings death to two of Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu. Moses tells Aaron and the surviving sons not to mourn. Instructions about wine and the priests' share of offerings follow.
The Blasphemer Stoned: A fight leads a man with Israelite and Egyptian parents to curse God's name. After seeking God's direction, the congregation stones him. The account restates equal justice for local people and foreign residents.
Counting the Camp: Israel's fighting-age men are counted by tribe at Sinai under God's command. Moses and Aaron gather the people for the census. Men must be at least twenty, and the Levites are excluded from this count.
Offerings and the Passover at Sinai: At Sinai, gifts from tribal leaders mark the altar's dedication, and the Levites begin their special service. Israel observes Passover, with a later date for those unclean. The cloud directs when the camp moves.
Leaving Sinai and the Complaints: Marching away from Sinai, Israel complains about manna and asks for meat. Seventy elders share the burden Moses carries. God sends quail, but a plague follows the arrival of the food.
Miriam and Aaron Speak Against Moses: Criticism from Miriam and Aaron concerns Moses's Ethiopian wife and his role as God's spokesman. God defends Moses. Miriam develops leprosy and must remain outside Israel's camp for a period of seven days.
The Twelve Spies: A scouting mission divides its twelve members over whether Israel should enter Canaan. Joshua and Caleb urge action, but ten oppose them. Israel rebels, and that generation faces forty years and death in the wilderness.
Korah's Rebellion: A challenge to Moses and Aaron ends with rebels swallowed by the ground and incense-bearers consumed by fire. Later, Aaron's staff grows buds. This sign confirms his priestly role after the revolt.
Water from the Rock at Meribah: Following Miriam's death, a water shortage brings another dispute. Moses hits the rock twice rather than speaking to it. God tells him and Aaron that they will not lead Israel into the land.
Edom Refuses Passage and Aaron Dies: Edom denies Israel permission to travel through its territory. Later, Aaron dies at Mount Hor. Before his death, his priestly clothes are placed on Eleazar, who receives them as Aaron's service ends.
The Bronze Serpent: After speaking against God and Moses, the people suffer bites from fiery snakes. Moses places a bronze serpent on a pole. Those who look toward it survive the bites they have received.
Victories over Sihon and Og: On its journey around Moab, Israel sings beside a well before facing two kings in battle. Victories over Sihon and Og bring the people control of their lands east of the Jordan River.
Balaam and Balak: A Moabite king seeks curses against Israel by hiring Balaam, whose donkey sees an angel on the road. Balaam instead speaks blessings. His final sayings include a coming star from Jacob.
Baal of Peor: Worship of Baal of Peor with Moabite women brings a plague upon Israel. Phinehas kills a man and a Midianite woman. The plague ends, and he receives a covenant of peace.
A New Census and Joshua Appointed: With a new generation counted, Israel also faces questions of inheritance and leadership. Zelophehad's daughters gain the right to inherit their father's property. Moses appoints Joshua to lead the people after him.
Vengeance on Midian: War against Midian brings the deaths of its kings and Balaam. Moses objects that women have been spared. The captured goods are divided, and the officers bring an offering for their own lives.
Tribes Settle East of the Jordan: Three tribal groups seek homes on the Jordan's eastern side: Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Moses grants the request with a condition. Their men must join the other tribes until the conquest ends.
Moses Recalls the Wilderness Years: Looking back from Moab, Moses reviews the failed entry into Canaan, the wilderness years and later victories. His request to enter the land is refused. Instead, he must prepare Joshua to lead Israel.
Moses Sets Apart Three Cities of Refuge: Bezer, Ramoth and Golan become places of refuge east of the Jordan. Moses designates them for someone who kills a neighbor by accident. The protection applies when there was no earlier hatred.
Moses Recalls the Golden Calf: In retelling the calf episode, Moses recalls breaking the stone tablets and destroying Israel's image. He also remembers pleading for Israel and Aaron. His prayers followed God's threat to destroy the people.
Moses Recalls the Second Tablets: Looking back, Moses describes preparing an ark and returning up the mountain with two new stone tablets. He places God's writing inside the ark. He also recalls pleading for Israel and receiving orders to continue.
Joshua Commissioned and the Law Entruste: Israel hears that Joshua will lead the crossing of the Jordan, and Moses encourages him publicly. Moses entrusts the written law to priests. He also teaches a song meant to remind the people of their duty.
The Death of Moses: From Mount Nebo, Moses views the land Israel is to enter but dies in Moab at 120. The people mourn for thirty days. Joshua, described as filled with wisdom, takes his place.
Joshua Commissioned: Leadership passes to Joshua after Moses's death, with a command to lead Israel across the Jordan. God urges courage and obedience to the law. The tribes settled in the east promise to follow him.
Rahab and the Spies: In Jericho, Rahab shelters Israel's spies and describes the city's fear of their God. She asks that her family be spared. A scarlet cord in her window will mark the home for protection.
Crossing the Jordan: The Jordan's flow stops when priests carrying the ark enter the river, opening a dry crossing for Israel. At Gilgal, twelve stones become a lasting reminder of the people's passage through the waters.
Circumcision and Passover at Gilgal: At Gilgal, men born during the wilderness journey are circumcised, and Israel observes Passover. Manna stops supplying their food. The commander of God's army then appears to Joshua near Jericho.
The Fall of Jericho: For seven days, Israel circles Jericho before a final shout brings down its walls. Rahab and her family are spared. The city itself is set apart for destruction after the walls fall.
Achan's Sin and Ai: Defeat at Ai follows Achan's theft of goods from Jericho that were set apart for destruction. He is identified and stoned. Israel then captures Ai through an ambush and renews the covenant.
The Gibeonite Deception: Pretending to come from far away, the Gibeonites secure a treaty with Israel. Discovery of their deception brings a new role. They must cut wood and carry water for the altar.
The Sun Stands Still: An attack on Gibeon draws Israel into battle against five Amorite kings. Hailstones strike the enemy at Beth-horon. Joshua calls for the sun and moon to stand still until Israel wins.
Northern Campaign and the Land Taken: Jabin of Hazor leads a northern alliance that Joshua defeats during Israel's campaign. The account then records conquered kings, setting out the victories won on both sides of the Jordan River.
Caleb Receives Hebron: At eighty-five, Caleb asks Joshua for the hill country where the Anakims live. He points to his earlier scouting report and Moses's promise. Joshua blesses Caleb and assigns him Hebron as his inheritance.
The Altar by the Jordan: An altar built beside the Jordan nearly brings war between Israel's eastern and western tribes. Phinehas leads a delegation to investigate. Its builders explain that it marks their connection, rather than serving for sacrifices.
Joshua's Farewell and Covenant at Sheche: In a final address, Joshua reviews God's dealings with Israel and asks the people to choose whom they will serve. They renew their covenant. The account closes with burials for Joshua, Joseph's bones and Eleazar.
Incomplete Conquest: Israel's tribes gain parts of the land while many Canaanite peoples remain in place. Their failure to drive these groups out is followed by a rebuke from God's angel at Bochim.
The Cycle of the Judges: A repeating pattern follows the death of Joshua's generation: Israel turns to other gods and suffers oppression. God raises judges to deliver the people. After each rescue, the same cycle begins again.
Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar: Three leaders confront Israel's enemies in different ways. Othniel defeats Cushan-rishathaim, while Ehud kills Eglon with a hidden blade and rallies Israel. Shamgar uses an oxgoad to kill six hundred Philistines.
Deborah and Barak: At Deborah's call, Barak goes to fight Sisera's force of chariots. Jael kills Sisera with a tent peg. Deborah and Barak then sing a song about the victory over their enemy.
Gideon and the Midianites: Called by an angel, Gideon destroys his father's Baal altar and seeks a sign through a fleece. With only three hundred men, trumpets and torches, he defeats Midian. He later refuses kingship.
Abimelech: After killing his brothers, Abimelech becomes king in Shechem, and Jotham responds with a fable. The city later turns against its king. A woman drops a millstone on Abimelech's head, leading to his death.
Jephthah's Vow: Before fighting Ammon, Jephthah vows to offer whatever first comes out of his house. His daughter is the one who appears. Later, conflict with Ephraim leads to fighting at the Jordan's crossings.
Samson: Set apart from birth, Samson battles the Philistines until Delilah's betrayal leads to his capture. His hair is cut and he is blinded. He later brings a temple down on himself and many Philistines.
Micah's Idols and the Danites: A shrine in Micah's household has idols and a Levite hired to serve there. The Danites take both the objects and the priest. They also seize Laish, a town described as peaceful.
The Levite and Gibeah: The fatal abuse of a Levite's concubine at Gibeah leads Israel to attack Benjamin. The fighting nearly destroys the tribe. Afterward, the other Israelites arrange wives for the men who have survived.
Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem: After famine sends Naomi's family to Moab, she loses her husband and both sons. She decides to return to Bethlehem. Ruth, one of her daughters-in-law, insists on going with her rather than leaving.
Ruth Gleans in Boaz's Field: Collecting leftover barley brings Ruth to a field owned by Boaz, a relative of Naomi's late husband. He treats Ruth kindly. Along with the grain she gathers, she receives extra grain from him.
The Threshing Floor: Following Naomi's advice, Ruth lies at Boaz's feet on the threshing floor. Boaz agrees to fulfill a close relative's duties, provided the nearer relative declines to do so.
Boaz Redeems and Marries Ruth: A decision at the city gate clears the way for Boaz to buy Elimelech's land and marry Ruth. Their son is named Obed. He later becomes the grandfather of David.
Hannah and the Birth of Samuel: At Shiloh, Hannah asks for a child and promises to dedicate a son to God. After Samuel's birth, she brings him to Eli. Her song gives thanks for the answer to her prayer.
Eli's Sons and Samuel's Call: Misconduct by Eli's sons brings a warning of judgment against their family from a man of God. Meanwhile, Samuel hears God calling during the night. The boy is confirmed as a prophet.
The Ark Captured and Returned: The Philistines capture Israel's ark, while Eli and his sons die. Plagues follow the ark through Philistine cities, prompting its return by cart. It eventually reaches Abinadab's house at Kirjath-jearim.
Samuel Judges Israel: At Mizpah, Samuel urges the people of Israel to give up their foreign gods. The LORD sends thunder against the Philistines. Samuel marks the victory with a stone called Ebenezer.
Israel Demands a King: Israel's elders request a king, and Saul of Benjamin is chosen and anointed. He defeats the Ammonites at Jabesh-gilead, confirming his rule. Samuel then gives his farewell address to Israel.
Saul Rejected: Two acts bring Saul into conflict with Samuel: an early sacrifice and spared Amalekite livestock. Saul also lets King Agag live. Samuel declares that Saul will lose the kingdom because of his actions.
David Anointed: Jesse's youngest son, David, receives Samuel's anointing in Bethlehem. He later enters the court of King Saul as a musician. When an evil spirit troubles Saul, David plays the lyre.
David and Goliath: For forty days, Goliath confronts Israel as the Philistines' champion. David goes out against him carrying five stones and a sling. He kills Goliath in the name of the LORD.
Saul's Jealousy and David's Flight: As David's success grows, Saul becomes jealous and tries to kill him. Jonathan has made an agreement with David and helps him escape. Michal and the priest Ahimelech also help David flee.
David in the Wilderness: While Saul pursues him, David gathers followers and twice spares the king's life. Saul orders the deaths of Nob's priests. Abigail steps in to stop David from killing her husband, Nabal.
Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Dea: At Endor, Saul consults a medium and is warned that he will die. Elsewhere, David defeats the Amalekites after being dismissed from the Philistine army. Saul and his sons die in battle on Mount Gilboa.
David Becomes King: After mourning Saul and Jonathan, David becomes king of Judah at Hebron. Abner and Ish-bosheth are later killed. The tribes of Israel then also anoint David as their king.
Jerusalem and the Ark: After taking Jerusalem, David brings the ark there in a transfer interrupted by Uzzah's death. The later arrival is celebrated with dancing. Michal scorns David for his part in the celebration.
The Davidic Covenant: David proposes building a house for the LORD. Through the prophet Nathan, God instead promises to establish David's house. The promise concerns David's throne, which God says will endure forever.
David and Mephibosheth: David's reign includes victories in wars on several fronts. He defeats the Ammonites and Arameans among his enemies. Alongside these campaigns, he shows kindness to Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan.
David, Bathsheba and Uriah: After taking Uriah's wife Bathsheba, David arranges for Uriah to die in battle. Nathan uses a parable to confront him, and David confesses. Bathsheba's first child dies; Solomon is later born.
Amnon, Tamar and Absalom: Tamar is raped by her half-brother Amnon, and Absalom has Amnon killed. Absalom then flees and remains away from Jerusalem. Joab later arranges for him to return to the city.
Absalom's Rebellion: David leaves Jerusalem after Absalom gains the people's support and leads a rebellion. The conflict ends with Absalom's death in the forest of Ephraim. David crosses the Jordan on his return.
Sheba's Revolt and the Gibeonites: Joab ends Sheba's northern revolt at Abel. A separate famine is linked to Saul's treatment of the Gibeonites. Seven of Saul's descendants are handed over in response to that earlier wrong.
The Exploits of David's Mighty Men: Three warriors risk their lives to bring David water from Bethlehem. He pours it out to the LORD rather than drinking it. Their deed appears alongside Benaiah's victories and other warriors' exploits.
The Census and the Plague: After ordering a count of Israel and Judah, David repents of what he has done. A plague then strikes Israel. David purchases Araunah's threshing floor as a place to build an altar.
Solomon Becomes King: As David ages, Adonijah attempts to claim the throne. Nathan and Bathsheba arrange for Solomon to be anointed instead. David gives Solomon his charge before dying, and Solomon removes his rivals.
Solomon's Wisdom: Solomon's request at Gibeon is for an understanding heart. His judgment in a dispute between two women over one child demonstrates his wisdom. The account describes the praise his wisdom receives.
The Temple Built: With supplies from Hiram of Tyre, Solomon constructs the temple and places the ark inside. He offers a prayer when the building is dedicated. The LORD's glory fills the new temple.
The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Decline: The queen of Sheba marvels at Solomon during her visit. Later, his many foreign wives turn him toward other gods. God raises opponents against Solomon as his reign takes this turn.
The Kingdom Divides: Rejecting advice from the elders, Rehoboam loses the support of Israel's northern tribes. They choose to follow Jeroboam instead. Jeroboam establishes golden calves at Bethel and Dan in the divided kingdom.
The Man of God from Judah: At Bethel, a prophet from Judah condemns Jeroboam's altar. The prophet later disobeys and dies in an encounter with a lion. Ahijah also declares that Jeroboam's royal house will come to an end.
Zimri's Coup and Omri's Rise: After Zimri kills Elah and Baasha's family, the army backs Omri for king. Zimri dies by burning the palace around himself. Omri overcomes a rival faction and builds the city of Samaria.
Elijah and the Drought: During the drought he announces, Elijah receives food from ravens and a widow at Zarephath. Her flour and oil continue to last. Elijah also restores the widow's son to life.
Elijah on Mount Carmel: A contest on Mount Carmel pits Elijah against the prophets of Baal. Fire consumes Elijah's sacrifice, and the prophets of Baal are killed. Rain then returns after the long drought.
Elijah at Horeb: Elijah escapes Jezebel's threat and reaches Horeb, where he hears the LORD's gentle whisper. He receives instructions to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha. He then calls Elisha to join him.
Naboth's Vineyard: Naboth's vineyard becomes the object of Ahab's desire. Jezebel arranges false charges that lead to Naboth being stoned to death. Elijah responds by announcing judgment against Ahab and his royal house.
Ahab and Micaiah: Before attacking Ramoth-gilead, Ahab and Jehoshaphat seek advice from prophets. Micaiah stands alone in predicting defeat rather than success. The battle goes ahead, and Ahab loses his life in the fighting.
Elijah Taken Up: Fire falls on soldiers sent to Elijah by King Ahaziah. Later, Elisha watches Elijah leave in a whirlwind and takes up his mantle. Elisha then heals the waters at Jericho.
Elisha and Moab: Three allied armies run out of water while marching against Moab. Elisha predicts both water and victory for Israel, Judah and Edom. Moab's king then sacrifices his son on the wall.
The Widow's Oil and the Shunammite's Son: Elisha helps a widow by multiplying her oil and restores another woman's son to life. He also makes a poisoned stew safe. Twenty loaves become enough to feed a hundred men.
Naaman Healed: Following instructions to wash seven times in the Jordan, the Aramean commander Naaman is healed. Elisha's servant Gehazi then accepts a reward. The skin disease that afflicted Naaman strikes Gehazi instead.
Elisha and the Arameans: Elisha recovers an axe head and brings blinded Aramean soldiers into Samaria. During a later siege, he predicts that it will end. Four men with skin disease find the Aramean camp deserted.
Jehu's Revolt: After being anointed by Elisha's messenger, Jehu kills the kings Joram and Ahaziah. He brings down Jezebel, Ahab's family and Baal's worshipers. Yet the golden calves remain under his rule.
Athaliah and Joash: Hidden in the temple, the infant Joash survives Athaliah's attack on the royal family. Six years later, the priest Jehoiada crowns him king. Joash then undertakes repairs to the temple.
Elisha's Death and Israel's Victories: After Elisha predicts victory and dies, a dead man revives on touching his bones. Jehoash defeats Judah's king Amaziah. Under Jeroboam II, Israel regains territory along its former borders.
The Fall of Samaria: Assyria's conquest of Samaria ends a succession of rulers as its people are taken away. New settlers then arrive in the land. They bring their own gods with them.
Hezekiah and Sennacherib: After Hezekiah removes local places of worship, Sennacherib's forces lay siege to his kingdom. Isaiah promises rescue from the Assyrians. The LORD's angel then strikes their camp during the invasion.
Hezekiah's Illness and the Babylonian En: Hezekiah receives healing and fifteen more years, marked by a shadow moving back ten steps. He later displays his riches to Babylonian visitors. Isaiah warns that exile will follow for Judah.
Manasseh, Amon and Josiah: Following the idol worship of Manasseh and Amon, Josiah renews Judah's agreement with God. A law book found in the temple prompts reforms and a great Passover. Josiah later dies at Megiddo.
The Fall of Jerusalem: Nebuchadnezzar's forces besiege Jerusalem, destroy its temple and take Judah's people into exile. Gedaliah is later killed. In Babylon, the imprisoned king Jehoiachin is eventually released after the fall of his kingdom.
The Death of Saul: The account places Saul's death alongside those of his sons on Mount Gilboa. The chronicler links his death to unfaithfulness. Saul's decision to consult a medium is among the reasons given.
David Takes Jerusalem and Gathers His Wa: At Hebron, the people of Israel make David their king. He goes on to capture Jerusalem. The account also names his leading warriors and records the troops who join him.
The Ark Brought to Jerusalem: An attempt to transport the ark by cart ends with Uzzah's death. David leaves it with Obed-edom before arranging another journey. Levites carry it into Jerusalem, where David appoints singers.
God's Covenant with David and His Wars: Nathan brings David God's promise that his royal line will last. The account also describes David's military campaigns. His victories include wars against the Philistines, Moab, Aram and Ammon during his reign.
The Census and the Temple Site: David counts Israel after Satan incites him, and a plague follows. He purchases Ornan's threshing floor and begins collecting temple materials. The planned temple will be built by his son Solomon.
David's Last Charge and Death: Solomon receives temple plans from David as the leaders offer gifts and David prays. Solomon is crowned for a second time. David then dies after forty years on the throne.
Solomon Builds the Temple: After asking for wisdom, Solomon builds the temple with help from Huram of Tyre. He brings in the ark and prays at its dedication. Fire and glory fill the completed building.
Solomon's Reign and the Queen of Sheba: During his reign, Solomon develops cities and organizes worship at the temple. He welcomes the queen of Sheba and receives tribute. The account closes this record of his reign with his death.
Rehoboam and the Division: A harsh reply from Rehoboam leads to the kingdom's division. In his fifth year as king, Jerusalem faces an attack by Shishak of Egypt. Rehoboam responds by humbling himself.
Abijah and Asa: Abijah defeats Jeroboam, while Asa removes idols and wins a battle against Zerah the Cushite. Later, Asa relies on Aram for help. He also turns to physicians rather than the LORD.
Jehoshaphat: Officials teach the law under Jehoshaphat, who also forms an alliance with Ahab. Later, Moab and Ammon threaten Judah together. Judah's people sing while the opposing forces turn on one another.
Jehoram, Ahaziah, Athaliah and Joash: Jehoram kills his brothers, and Athaliah later takes the throne. Jehoiada replaces her by crowning Joash. After the priest's death, Joash turns away from God and orders Zechariah to be stoned.
Amaziah, Uzziah and Jotham: Amaziah adopts Edom's gods after defeating its people. Uzziah later prospers but develops a skin disease after entering the temple to burn incense. The account contrasts these rulers with Jotham's faithful reign.
Ahaz and Hezekiah's Reforms: After Ahaz shuts the temple and sacrifices to foreign gods, Hezekiah reverses his policies. He opens and cleanses the temple, restoring its worship. He also invites all Israel to celebrate Passover.
Sennacherib's Invasion and Hezekiah's Pr: Facing Sennacherib's invasion, Hezekiah strengthens Jerusalem's defenses and prepares its water supply. The Assyrian army is then struck down. Later in his reign, Hezekiah becomes proud but is brought low.
Manasseh's Repentance and Josiah's Refor: Captivity in Babylon leads Manasseh to humble himself and remove idols after returning. Josiah later renews the covenant following the law book's discovery. He celebrates Passover before dying in battle against Pharaoh Necho.
The Fall of Judah and Cyrus's Decree: Babylon's conquest ends Judah's monarchy and leaves the temple burned. The land remains desolate for seventy years. Cyrus, the Persian king, then issues an order allowing the temple to be rebuilt.
Cyrus's Decree and the Return: A Persian royal decree opens the way for exiles to return and rebuild Jerusalem's temple. Cyrus also gives back its vessels. The returning people are listed under their leaders, Zerubbabel and Jeshua.
Rebuilding the Altar and Foundation: Back in Jerusalem, the people restore the altar and celebrate the Feast of Booths. They then lay the foundation for the temple. Shouts of joy mingle with weeping from the older generation.
Opposition and Delay: Refused a role in rebuilding the temple, opponents block the work. Later letters also halt construction in Jerusalem under Artaxerxes. The account returns to the temple's delay until Darius's reign.
The Temple Completed: Prophets Haggai and Zechariah call for temple construction to begin again. Darius confirms Cyrus's earlier decree and provides support for the work. The finished temple is dedicated, and the people celebrate Passover.
Ezra Comes to Jerusalem: With authority from King Artaxerxes, Ezra prepares to bring a group of exiles to Jerusalem. The priest and scribe leads them in fasting for safe travel. They then make the journey.
Ezra and Mixed Marriages: Reports of marriages to foreign women leave Ezra deeply troubled. He turns to prayer over the marriages among the people of Israel. The gathered community then agrees to send the foreign wives away.
Nehemiah's Prayer and Commission: News of Jerusalem's broken walls reaches Nehemiah while he serves as the king's cupbearer. After praying, he seeks permission from Artaxerxes to go rebuild. He also requests letters for his journey.
Rebuilding the Wall: After a night inspection, Nehemiah gathers the people to repair Jerusalem's ruined wall. Sanballat and Tobiah mock the effort and make threats. Guards are posted, and the builders work with weapons.
Debt Relief: Debt costs poor families their land and even their children. Nehemiah confronts the nobles, who agree to return what they have taken. He also declines the food allowance provided for the governor.
The Wall Completed: Despite plots directed against Nehemiah, Jerusalem's wall is completed in fifty-two days. The account then turns to a recovered register. It records the people who had returned from exile.
Ezra Reads the Law: The gathered people hear Ezra read the law while Levites explain its meaning. They celebrate the Feast of Booths. A later prayer recalls Israel's history as the people confess their sins.
The Dedication of Jerusalem’s Wall: Two groups walk along Jerusalem's wall giving thanks at its dedication. Levites and singers join the occasion, and both groups meet at God's house. Sacrifices and celebration follow the procession.
Nehemiah's Reforms: Returning from Persia, Nehemiah finds several matters to address in Jerusalem. He removes Tobiah from temple space, restores tithes and closes the Sabbath gates. He also confronts marriages to foreign women.
Vashti Deposed: During a long royal feast, Queen Vashti declines King Ahasuerus's order to appear before him. The king turns to his counselors for advice. Following their counsel, he removes her as queen.
Esther Becomes Queen: Raised by her cousin Mordecai, Esther becomes queen while keeping her Jewish identity private. Mordecai then uncovers a plan against the king. His discovery brings the plot to the king's attention.
Haman's Plot: Mordecai's refusal to bow prompts Haman to seek a decree against all Jews. Mordecai asks Esther to act on their behalf. She calls for the Jewish people to fast before she intervenes.
Esther's Banquets: Two banquets allow Esther to reveal Haman's actions to the king. Meanwhile, the king honors Mordecai for his earlier service. Haman is hanged on the gallows he had built.
The Jews Delivered and Purim: Permission to defend themselves allows the Jews to defeat those attacking them. Purim is established to mark these days. Mordecai also gains a high position after the threat to his people passes.
Job's Testing: Satan challenges Job's motives, and Job loses his possessions, children and health. His wife urges him to curse God. Three friends arrive to sit with him in the midst of his losses.
Elihu Speaks: When Job's three friends stop speaking, the younger Elihu takes his turn. He challenges Job for declaring himself right. He also faults the friends for failing to give Job an answer.
God Answers from the Whirlwind: From a whirlwind, God speaks to Job with questions about the world he created. His questions turn to different animals and include the beings named Behemoth and Leviathan.
Job Restored: Job admits that he spoke about matters beyond his understanding. God rebukes the three friends, and Job prays for them. His wealth is doubled, and he becomes the father of more children.
Isaiah's Call: Isaiah sees the LORD on a throne in the year of King Uzziah's death. A heavenly being called a seraph touches his lips with a coal. Isaiah is sent to people who will not understand.
Ahaz and the Sign of Immanuel: With Syria and Israel threatening Judah, Isaiah urges Ahaz to remain firm. Ahaz declines to request a sign. Isaiah announces that a virgin will bear a son who will be named Immanuel.
Sennacherib's Threat and Hezekiah: An Assyrian commander calls for Jerusalem to surrender during Sennacherib's campaign. Hezekiah lays the king's threatening letter before the LORD. Isaiah promises rescue, and the Assyrian camp is struck down.
Hezekiah's Illness: Facing death, Hezekiah prays and receives another fifteen years of life. Later, he displays his treasures to visitors from Babylon. Isaiah warns that those riches will eventually be taken there.
Jeremiah's Call: Jeremiah receives his call to speak to the nations while still young. God shows him an almond branch and a boiling pot. He is told not to fear the task ahead.
The Potter's House and the Broken Jar: At a potter's workshop, Jeremiah sees a spoiled vessel shaped again into a new one. He later breaks a clay jar in the Valley of Hinnom. The broken jar announces coming destruction.
Jeremiah and Pashhur: Pashhur has Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks. Once released, Jeremiah declares that judgment will fall on the priest. He also voices bitter complaints about the calling he has received.
Hananiah's False Prophecy: Hananiah breaks Jeremiah's yoke and predicts freedom from Babylon within two years. Jeremiah responds with a warning about an iron yoke. Hananiah dies before that same year is over.
The Scroll Burned: Jeremiah's words reach the temple through a scroll written and read by Baruch. Jehoiakim cuts up the scroll and burns it. Jeremiah dictates another version, adding further words to the record.
Jeremiah in the Cistern: While Jerusalem is under siege, Jeremiah is imprisoned in a cistern filled with mud. Ebed-melech, a Cushite, brings him out. King Zedekiah later speaks with Jeremiah in a private meeting.
The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egyp: Freed after Babylon takes Jerusalem, Jeremiah warns survivors against going to Egypt. Gedaliah's death is followed by their decision to flee there anyway. They take Jeremiah with them as they leave.
Ezekiel's Vision and Commission: Ezekiel's vision beside the Chebar canal includes four living creatures and wheels. He receives a scroll and is told to eat it. His commission makes him a watchman for the people of Israel.
The Glory Leaves the Temple: Idolatry fills the temple in Ezekiel's vision, and the LORD's glory leaves the city. Yet God promises the scattered exiles a return and a new heart when he gathers them.
The Death of Ezekiel's Wife: Ezekiel's wife dies after the LORD warns him of her death and forbids the usual mourning rites. His response becomes a sign to the people about the sanctuary and their families.
The Valley of Dry Bones: Dry bones become living people in a vision that pictures Israel's restoration. Ezekiel also joins two sticks, showing that Judah and Israel will be brought together as a single kingdom.
Ezekiel Is Shown the Temple in a Vision: From a high mountain in Israel, Ezekiel sees a man holding a measuring reed at a gate. He must watch what the vision shows and report it to the people of Israel.
Daniel and His Friends in Babylon: Four captives brought to Babylon must train for service under Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel and his friends refuse the royal food, thrive on vegetables and water, and enter the king's service together.
Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Statue: A king demands both the content and meaning of his dream, and God reveals them to Daniel. The dream's shattered statue represents kingdoms that will give way to God's kingdom.
The Fiery Furnace: Refusing to worship the king's golden image sends Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego into a blazing furnace. A fourth figure appears beside them, and all three emerge from the fire without harm.
Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling: A dream about a great tree being cut down receives an explanation from Daniel. Nebuchadnezzar then loses his sanity for seven periods before recovering and offering his praise to God.
Belshazzar's Feast: Writing appears on a wall at Belshazzar's feast, and Daniel interprets it as judgment on his kingdom. That night the king is killed, and rule passes to Darius the Median.
Daniel in the Lions' Den: A decree obtained by jealous officials makes Daniel's prayers illegal, but he continues praying. He is thrown into a den of lions and later found alive, without harm from them.
Daniel's Visions: Beasts, a ram, a goat and a son of man appear in Daniel's visions. He also receives an answer about seventy weeks and a final vision concerning kings and the end.
Hosea's Marriage to Gomer: Hosea takes Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, as his wife at the LORD's command. Their children's names, Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, carry symbolic messages concerning the people of Israel and Judah.
Amaziah Opposes Amos: Amos faces a demand from the priest Amaziah to leave Bethel and speak in Judah instead. He replies that the LORD called him from herding and announces judgment against the priest.
Jonah Flees and Is Swallowed: A voyage away from Nineveh brings Jonah into a storm, and the sailors throw him overboard. Swallowed by a great fish, he prays before being cast back onto dry land.
Nineveh Repents: Nineveh's people respond to Jonah's preaching by repenting, with the king joining them in wearing sackcloth. God then relents, and the disaster announced against the city does not take place.
Jonah's Anger: Nineveh is spared, leaving Jonah angry at God's decision. A plant shades him, then withers. The LORD compares Jonah's concern for the plant with God's own concern for the city.
The Birth of Jesus and the Magi: A dream tells Joseph that Mary's child comes from the Holy Spirit. Guided by a star, visiting magi travel to Bethlehem and present their gifts to the child they find there.
Flight to Egypt and Return to Nazareth: Joseph takes his family to safety in Egypt after a warning dream, while Herod kills boys in Bethlehem. Herod's death allows the family to return, and they make their home in Nazareth.
The Baptism and Temptation of Jesus: At Jesus's baptism in the Jordan, a voice speaks from heaven. He then fasts for forty days in the wilderness, where he responds to three temptations from the devil with scripture.
Calling the First Disciples: Simon, Andrew, James and John receive a call to follow Jesus as he begins preaching in Galilee. His work also draws crowds of people who come to him for healing.
Healings and Calming the Storm: A series of healings includes a leper, a servant, Peter's mother-in-law and a paralytic. Jesus calms a storm, sends demons into pigs, calls Matthew, raises a girl and heals a woman.
Sending Out the Twelve: The twelve disciples receive authority to heal disease and drive out unclean spirits before Jesus sends them out. The list of those chosen includes Judas Iscariot, who will later betray him.
Jesus and John the Baptist: From prison, John sends followers to ask Jesus if he is the expected one. Jesus points them to his works and extends an invitation to weary people to come to him.
Sabbath Controversies and the Sign of Jo: Questions about the Sabbath follow the disciples' grain picking and Jesus's healing of a man's hand. Jesus defends his disciples and later answers a demand for a sign by pointing to Jonah.
Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on: After Herod has John the Baptist beheaded, Jesus feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish. He later walks on the sea, where Peter briefly steps out toward him.
Peter's Confession and the Transfigurati: Peter identifies Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus speaks of his coming death and resurrection. Six days afterward, Peter, James and John see Jesus changed in appearance during the transfiguration.
The Rich Young Man: Possessions keep a rich young man from following Jesus when asked to give them up. Jesus also tells a story about vineyard workers and restores the sight of two men near Jericho.
The Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing: A donkey carries Jesus into Jerusalem, where he removes merchants from the temple. He also curses a fig tree and responds when others challenge the authority behind what he does.
The Last Supper and Gethsemane: A woman anoints Jesus, and Judas agrees to betray him. Jesus shares a Passover meal with the twelve. He then prays in Gethsemane, where Judas arrives with an armed crowd.
Trial, Crucifixion and Burial: Trials before Caiaphas and Pilate lead to Jesus's crucifixion, while Peter denies him and Judas dies. After Jesus dies on the cross, his body is placed in Joseph of Arimathea's tomb.
The Resurrection and the Great Commissio: Women discover an empty tomb and meet Jesus after his resurrection. Guards are paid to spread a false story. Jesus sends the eleven to make disciples among people of all nations.
John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesu: John calls for repentance in the wilderness and baptizes Jesus, with the Spirit descending upon him. A period of testing follows, as Jesus spends forty days in the wilderness.
Calling the Disciples and Healing in Cap: Four fishermen become followers of Jesus as he calls them to join him. He also removes an unclean spirit in a synagogue, heals Peter's mother-in-law and cleanses a man with leprosy.
The Paralytic and Controversies: A man lowered through a roof by four friends receives forgiveness and healing from Jesus. Jesus also calls Levi, defends his disciples' Sabbath conduct and heals a man with a withered hand.
Parables and Calming the Storm: Beside the sea, Jesus teaches through stories, including those of a sower and a mustard seed. The account then moves onto the lake, where Jesus brings a storm to an end.
The Gadarene Demoniac, Jairus and the Wo: A man is freed when Jesus sends a legion of demons into a herd of pigs. In other encounters, a woman is healed after touching his cloak, and Jairus's daughter is raised.
Feeding the Multitude: Jesus provides food for a crowd of five thousand people. He later reaches his disciples on the lake, making his way to them by walking across the water.
Peter's Confession and the Transfigurati: After Peter identifies him as the Christ, Jesus speaks about the suffering ahead of him. A change in his appearance on a mountain precedes his healing of a boy with an unclean spirit.
Blind Bartimaeus: Near Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus calls out to Jesus, addressing him as the son of David. The encounter ends with the beggar receiving his sight after calling to him.
Triumphal Entry and the Temple: Riding a colt, Jesus arrives in Jerusalem and later removes the traders from the temple. He also curses a fig tree and faces questions about his authority to do these things.
The Last Supper and Gethsemane in Mark: At Bethany a woman anoints Jesus, while Judas makes arrangements to betray him. Jesus shares a final supper with his followers, then prays in Gethsemane, where he is placed under arrest.
Trial, Crucifixion and Burial in Mark: The council and Pilate try Jesus, while Peter denies knowing him. Jesus is then crucified between two criminals, and his body is later buried by Joseph of Arimathea.
The Empty Tomb: A rolled-away stone meets the women arriving at Jesus's tomb. Inside, a young man announces that Jesus has risen, and the women run away in fear after hearing his words.
The Births of John and Jesus: Gabriel announces two births, speaking to Zechariah about John and to Mary about Jesus. Mary visits Elizabeth, and John is born before Jesus's birth in Bethlehem, where shepherds visit him.
Presentation and the Boy Jesus in the Te: The infant Jesus is seen by Simeon and Anna during a visit to the temple. Years later, at twelve, he remains in Jerusalem and is found there among the teachers.
Rejection at Nazareth: A reading from Isaiah in Nazareth's synagogue leads Jesus to announce that its words are fulfilled. The crowd turns against him and attempts to throw him down from a cliff.
The Miraculous Catch: An unsuccessful night's fishing changes when Simon lowers his nets at Jesus's direction. The catch is so large that the boats begin to sink, and Simon leaves everything to follow Jesus.
The Centurion and the Widow's Son: Two encounters concern a servant belonging to a centurion and a widow's only son in Nain. Jesus heals the servant from a distance and raises the widow's son from the dead.
The Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus: A meal at a Pharisee's house includes a woman washing Jesus's feet with tears and oil. Jesus responds with a story about two people in debt and grants the woman forgiveness.
The Good Samaritan and Mary and Martha: A question about neighbors prompts Jesus to tell of a Samaritan helping a traveler who has been beaten. Later, Martha welcomes Jesus, and Mary sits at his feet during the visit.
The Lost Sheep, Coin and Son: Three stories told by Jesus concern what was lost and then recovered: a sheep, a coin and a son. The account of the returning son also includes the response of his elder brother.
The Rich Man and Lazarus: In a story told by Jesus, Lazarus is poor while another man has wealth. Their circumstances after death are the reverse of those they experienced during their lives on earth.
Zacchaeus: To get a view of Jesus, Zacchaeus climbs into a tree. The tax collector then receives Jesus at his home and commits to paying back the people he has cheated.
The Road to Emmaus: Travelers on the road to Emmaus speak with Jesus after his resurrection but do not know who he is. Breaking bread reveals his identity to them, and they go back to Jerusalem.
The Ascension: Jesus appears to the disciples and helps them understand what the scriptures say. As he gives them his blessing, he is taken up into heaven and departs from their sight.
The First Disciples and the Wedding at C: Andrew and another disciple begin following Jesus, and Philip and Nathanael also become part of the group. Later, a wedding in Cana is the setting where Jesus turns water into wine.
Cleansing the Temple and Nicodemus: During Passover, Jesus clears merchants out of the temple. Nicodemus later comes to him at night. Their conversation includes Jesus's teaching that a person must be born again.
The Woman at the Well: A request for a drink begins Jesus's conversation with a Samaritan woman at a well. He speaks to her about living water, and many people in her town come to believe.
Healing at Bethesda: At Bethesda's pool, a man who has spent thirty-eight years ill receives healing from Jesus on the Sabbath. Jesus follows this act by speaking about his relationship with the Father.
Bread of Life: Feeding five thousand and walking on the sea lead into Jesus's teaching at Capernaum. He describes himself as the bread of life, but many of his disciples turn away from him.
The Woman Caught in Adultery: Accusers bring an adulterous woman to Jesus and ask whether she should be stoned. He tells whoever is without sin to cast the first stone, then sends the woman away.
The Man Born Blind: Sight comes to a man who has been blind from birth after Jesus heals him. The Pharisees question both the man and his parents, then cast the healed man out.
Jesus at the Feast of Dedication: Questions about whether Jesus is the Christ turn to threats of stoning at Jerusalem's Feast of Dedication. He escapes an attempt to seize him and goes beyond Jordan, where many believe.
The Raising of Lazarus: Four days after Lazarus of Bethany is placed in a tomb, Jesus raises him from the dead. The council then reaches a decision that Jesus himself must be put to death.
Anointing and Triumphal Entry: An anointing by Mary takes place six days ahead of Passover. Jesus then rides a donkey into Jerusalem, and a group of Greeks express their wish to see him there.
Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet: At supper, Jesus washes his disciples' feet and tells them to serve one another. He identifies Judas as his betrayer by handing him food. He also predicts that Peter will deny him three times.
Arrest, Trial and Crucifixion: An arrest in a garden leads to Jesus being questioned by Annas and Pilate before his crucifixion. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus then take part in burying him after his death.
The Resurrection Appearances: An empty tomb precedes Mary Magdalene's encounter with Jesus after his resurrection. He also visits his disciples, and Thomas comes to believe when he sees the wounds on Jesus's body.
Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias: A night spent fishing is followed by an appearance of Jesus to seven disciples beside the sea. He eats with them and asks Peter three times whether he loves him.
The Ascension and the Replacement of Jud: A promise of the Holy Spirit comes before Jesus is taken up from the apostles. They later cast lots to select a replacement for Judas, and Matthias is chosen for that place.
Pentecost: Believers begin speaking other languages as the Spirit comes upon them. Peter's preaching is followed by the baptism of about three thousand people, and the growing community shares its possessions.
The Lame Man Healed and Arrest of Peter: A man unable to walk is healed at the temple gate by Peter and John. After arrest, they speak boldly to the council, while the believers pray together for courage.
Ananias and Sapphira: Shared property forms part of the believers' life together, but one couple gives a false account of a sale. Ananias and Sapphira both die after lying about the price of their field.
Stephen: The choice of seven men to serve widows introduces Stephen's role among the believers. He faces an accusation of blasphemy, recounts Israel's history in a speech and is killed by stoning.
Philip and the Ethiopian: As persecution scatters the church, Philip takes his preaching to Samaria. He also meets an Ethiopian official, explains a passage from Isaiah to him and baptizes him after their conversation.
Saul's Conversion: A journey to arrest believers in Damascus is interrupted when a heavenly light blinds Saul. Ananias then restores his sight, and Saul begins speaking publicly about Jesus instead of arresting followers.
Peter, Cornelius and the Gentiles: A vision featuring unclean animals precedes Peter's visit to Cornelius, a centurion. The Spirit comes upon this Gentile household, and the church in Jerusalem accepts what has happened among them.
Peter's Escape and Herod's Death: James is killed and Peter imprisoned under Herod, but an angel frees Peter. Later, an angel strikes Herod after people call his voice divine and he gives God no glory. Herod dies.
Paul's First Journey: A mission from Antioch takes Barnabas and Saul to Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch and Lystra to preach. Paul is stoned in Lystra, and they later return to appoint elders among the believers.
The Jerusalem Council: Whether Gentile believers must undergo circumcision brings the apostles and elders together for a council. Their decision is sent in a letter that sets out only a few requirements for those believers.
Paul in Philippi: After Timothy joins Paul, a call leads Paul to Macedonia, where Lydia believes. Paul and Silas are jailed in Philippi, an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer is baptized before their release.
Thessalonica, Athens and Corinth: Thessalonica and Berea hear Paul's preaching as he travels through their communities. In Athens he addresses the Areopagus, and his journey also takes him to Corinth, where he stays for eighteen months.
Ephesus: A riot led by silversmiths follows about two years of Paul's teaching in Ephesus. Later, Paul raises Eutychus at Troas. He also bids farewell to the elders from Ephesus.
Paul Arrested in Jerusalem: Paul's visit to Jerusalem ends with his seizure in the temple and an address to the crowd. He is brought before the council, then transferred to Caesarea after a plot against him.
Paul Before Felix, Festus and Agrippa: Felix, Festus and King Agrippa each hear Paul's defense as he appears before them. During these proceedings, he also makes an appeal for his case to be heard by Caesar.
Shipwreck and Rome: A voyage toward Rome brings Paul through a storm and a shipwreck at Malta. He survives, reaches Rome and continues his preaching there even while he is living under house arrest.
